cite_role: 2x2 exemplar: outcome × averaged (standard RLHF)
title: Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback
authors: Long Ouyang et al.
summary: InstructGPT: aligns LLMs to instructions via supervised fine-tuning and RLHF from labeler rankings.
usil_relation: Canonical averaged-outcome alignment (the averaged/outcome cell of the 2x2).

cite_role: 2x2 exemplar: outcome × individual (latent user variable)
title: Personalizing Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback with Variational Preference Learning
authors: Sriyash Poddar, Yanming Wan, Hamish Ivison, Abhishek Gupta, Natasha Jaques
summary: Infers a latent user variable from a few preference labels and conditions the reward model and policy on it.
usil_relation: Latent-variable personalization for outcomes; open question is whether the same machinery can condition interaction decisions (ask/act).

cite_role: 2x2 exemplar: outcome × individual, few-shot personalization
title: FSPO: Few-Shot Optimization of Synthetic Preferences Personalizes to Real Users
authors: Anikait Singh, Sheryl Hsu, Kyle Hsu, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Tatsunori Hashimoto, Archit Sharma, Chelsea Finn
summary: Meta-learns few-shot preference optimization on synthetic users and transfers to real users.
usil_relation: Strongest few-shot personalization result; remaining question is few-shot adaptation of interaction policies rather than responses.

cite_role: 2x2 exemplar: procedure × averaged; act/ask utility threshold used in the toy model
title: Principles of Mixed-Initiative User Interfaces
authors: Eric Horvitz
summary: Decision-theoretic principles for when an agent should act, ask (engage in dialog), or do nothing, based on expected utility and uncertainty.
usil_relation: The act-ask threshold USIL builds on; USIL asks how per-user costs are learned from sparse evidence.

cite_role: Autonomy treated as a fixed design choice (the practice the position argues against)
title: Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents
authors: K. J. Kevin Feng, David W. McDonald, Amy X. Zhang
summary: Defines five levels of agent autonomy by the user's role (operator to observer) as a design choice.
usil_relation: Treats autonomy as a fixed design choice; USIL asks whether it should be learned per user and context.

cite_role: Task-success evaluation with users in the loop (contrast case)
title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
authors: Shunyu Yao, Noah Shinn, Pedram Razavi, Karthik Narasimhan
summary: Benchmark of tool-using agents interacting with simulated users under domain policies.
usil_relation: Task-success evaluation with users in the loop, but no per-user adaptation.

cite_role: Key evidence: individual differences explain ~half of delegation variance (ICC=.50)
title: Delegating or Doing? Understanding User Behavior in Hybrid Human-Agent Interfaces
authors: Gavin Dizon, Tyrone Justin Sta Maria, Jordan Aiko Deja, Yasuyuki Sumi
summary: Between-subjects study (N=73) of a web CMS where users either act through direct manipulation or delegate to an MCP-connected LLM agent (traditional-only, AI-first, and hybrid modes). Delegation did not follow operation risk. It varied far more between users than between tasks: individual differences explained about half the variance in assistant use (ICC = .50).
what_is_learned: other: none learned (empirical characterization of per-user delegation tendencies)
user_evidence: per-user choice to delegate vs. directly manipulate, interaction logs (clicks, navigation, scrolling), task outcomes
usil_relation: Direct empirical support for USIL's premise that delegation is a property of the user more than of the task. Open question: can an agent estimate this user-level delegation tendency from a few early interactions and adjust its own initiative to match?

cite_role: Evidence: delegation regret when agents act beyond authorization
title: Assistant or Actor? Student Trust, Control, and Delegation Regret When Using a General-Purpose AI Agent
authors: Shiva Pochampally, Shengwei An, Yan Chen
summary: User study of delegation to a general-purpose agent, documenting regret over actions beyond what users would authorize.
usil_relation: Evidence that acting beyond authorization harms users even when outcomes are correct.

cite_role: Evidence: distinct individual intervention styles with web agents
title: Modeling Distinct Human Interaction in Web Agents
authors: Faria Huq, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Zhanqiu Guo, Venu Arvind Arangarajan, Tianyue Ou, Frank Xu, Shuyan Zhou, Graham Neubig, Jeffrey P. Bigham
summary: Characterizes distinct human intervention styles when supervising web agents and models them to predict interventions.
usil_relation: Close predecessor showing individual intervention styles; open question is adapting the agent's own policy to each style.

cite_role: Evidence: individual model rankings diverge from aggregate rankings
title: Personalized Benchmarking: Evaluating LLMs by Individual Preferences
authors: Cristina Garbacea, Heran Wang, Chenhao Tan
summary: Shows per-user model rankings diverge from aggregate rankings and proposes individual-level evaluation.
usil_relation: Evidence that averaged evaluation misrepresents individuals—extends naturally to interaction behavior.

cite_role: Evidence: no single oversight strategy is best for all users
title: Comparing Human Oversight Strategies for Computer-Use Agents
authors: Chaoran Chen, Zhiping Zhang, Zeya Chen, et al.
summary: Mixed-methods study (N=48) in a live web environment that compares four oversight strategies for LLM computer-use agents, which differ in delegation structure and engagement level. Strategy mainly changed whether users saw problematic actions, not whether they could correct them once seen. No strategy was best for everyone. Effective oversight depends on bringing decision-critical moments to the surface rather than maximizing human involvement.
what_is_learned: other: none learned (comparison of fixed oversight/interaction designs)
user_evidence: interventions/corrections during execution, exposure to risky actions, trust and subjective ratings, qualitative interviews
interaction_decisions: confirm, intervene, ask (plan approval vs. step-level oversight)
usil_relation: Shows that the right confirmation and intervention structure depends on context and on how recognizable risky moments are, which is what USIL's ask/act/confirm policy decides. Open question: can an agent learn per user which moments that user treats as decision-critical, instead of using one fixed oversight strategy?

cite_role: Trust and reliance evolve with experience (why preferences drift)
title: Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance
authors: John D. Lee, Katrina A. See
summary: Review of how trust in automation forms, evolves with experience, and governs reliance.
usil_relation: Explains why desired autonomy changes over time (P5/P1 drift).

cite_role: Historical precedent: personalized, learned cost of interruption (BusyBody)
title: BusyBody: Creating and Fielding Personalized Models of the Cost of Interruption
authors: Eric Horvitz; Paul Koch; Johnson Apacible
summary: Learns context-sensitive individual interruption costs and deploys notifications
usil_relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P3;P4; capabilities require full-text verification.

cite_role: Formal deference under uncertainty
title: The Off-Switch Game
authors: Dylan Hadfield-Menell, Anca Dragan, Pieter Abbeel, Stuart Russell
summary: Shows uncertainty about human preferences incentivizes an agent to defer to human oversight.
usil_relation: Formal model of deference; USIL adds individual variation in desired oversight.

cite_role: Changing and influenceable preferences: limits on legitimate adaptation
title: AI Alignment with Changing and Influenceable Reward Functions
authors: Micah Carroll, Davis Foote, Anand Siththaranjan, Stuart Russell, Anca Dragan
summary: Formalizes alignment when user preferences change over time and can be influenced by the AI system.
usil_relation: Key reference for preference drift and influence; USIL inherits the question of which adaptation is legitimate.

cite_role: Decision-theoretic confirmation frequency (population-level)
title: When Should Users Check? Modeling Confirmation Frequency in Multi-Step Agentic AI Tasks
authors: Jieyu Zhou, Aryan Roy, Sneh Gupta, Daniel Weitekamp, Christopher J. MacLellan
summary: Decision-theoretic model of how often users should confirm agent steps in multi-step tasks.
usil_relation: Directly models confirmation; open question is learning the schedule per user.

cite_role: Value-of-information rule for when to ask (population costs)
title: Value of Information: A Framework for Human–Agent Communication
authors: Yijiang River Dong, Tiancheng Hu, Zheng Hui, Caiqi Zhang, Ivan Vulić, Andreea Bobu, Nigel Collier
summary: Uses value of information to decide when agents should communicate or ask users.
usil_relation: Principled when-to-ask rule with population-level costs; per-user costs are the USIL gap.

cite_role: Origin: learning interface agents (Maes 1994)
title: Agents that Reduce Work and Information Overload
authors: Pattie Maes
summary: Foundational learning interface agents; slightly before the requested 1995 boundary
usil_relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P2; capabilities require full-text verification.

cite_role: Early per-user interaction profile: warn/suggest/act, interruption timing
title: User–interface agent interaction: personalization issues
authors: Silvia Schiaffino, Analía Amandi
summary: Argues interface agents should personalize the interaction itself—assistance type (warn, suggest, act), interruption timing, error tolerance—stored in a user interaction profile.
user_evidence: observed user reactions and explicit feedback
usil_relation: Earliest direct predecessor of USIL's interaction-policy framing; pre-LLM and rule/learning-based—how does it scale to tool-using LLM agents?

cite_role: Essential historical predecessor: early formulation of learning when and how an interface agent should interact with each individual user
title: Personalizing User–Agent Interaction
authors: Silvia Schiaffino; Analía Amandi
summary: Direct statement to learn how to interact with each user; assistance timing/type
usil_relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P2;P3; capabilities require full-text verification.

cite_role: Historical follow-up: user-adapted assistance and interaction timing; compare with earlier user-agent interaction work
title: Building respectful interface agents
authors: Silvia Schiaffino, Marcelo Armentano, Analía Amandi
summary: Interface agents that learn when and how to interrupt or assist each user without being intrusive.
usil_relation: Per-user interruption learning predates LLM agents; open question is extension to consequential actions.

cite_role: HRI line: mutual adaptation in shared autonomy
title: Human-Robot Mutual Adaptation in Shared Autonomy
summary: Robot adapts to users who may adapt back; preferences versus trust and performance
usil_relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P2;P3; capabilities require full-text verification.

cite_role: Learning latent preferences from user edits
title: Aligning LLM Agents by Learning Latent Preference from User Edits
authors: Ge Gao, Alexey Taymanov, Eduardo Salinas, Paul Mineiro, Dipendra Misra
summary: PRELUDE/CIPHER infers latent user preferences from edits to agent outputs and conditions future generations.
usil_relation: Learns from naturally occurring edits over time; affects what is produced, not when to ask or act.

cite_role: Persistent general user models from computer use
title: Creating General User Models from Computer Use
authors: Omar Shaikh, Shardul Sapkota, Shan Rizvi, Eric Horvitz, Joon Sung Park, Diyi Yang, Michael S. Bernstein
summary: Builds general user models (GUM) from unstructured computer-use observations as confidence-weighted propositions.
usil_relation: Rich persistent user model; how such a model should drive ask/act decisions is open.

cite_role: Learning when to ask/suggest, but for a population
title: CollabLLM: From Passive Responders to Active Collaborators
authors: Shirley Wu, Michel Galley, Baolin Peng, et al.
summary: Argues next-turn reward makes LLMs passive; trains with a multiturn-aware reward estimated by simulating future collaboration with a user simulator, so the model learns to clarify intent and make suggestions. Introduces a multiturn collaboration benchmark and a 201-person user study (higher satisfaction, less time).
user_evidence: Simulated user responses over future turns (rollouts) scored for task success, efficiency and engagement; no real per-user data in training
interaction_decisions: ask, clarify, suggest (proactive intervention) vs. answer
usil_relation: Learns a population-level when-to-ask/suggest policy via long-horizon reward; open question is whether the multiturn-aware reward can be conditioned on an individual user's history so that clarification frequency adapts per user.

cite_role: User-conditioned assistance policy learned with offline RL
title: Towards Optimizing Human-Centric Objectives in AI-Assisted Decision-Making With Offline Reinforcement Learning
authors: Zana Buçinca, Siddharth Swaroop, Amanda E. Paluch, Susan A. Murphy, Krzysztof Z. Gajos
summary: Frames the choice of what kind of AI assistance to give (e.g., recommendation, explanation, none) as offline RL over human–AI interaction data. The learned policy adapts assistance to the person and context to optimize human-centric objectives. In two experiments (N=316, N=964), accuracy-optimized policies beat fixed assistance types and reached human–AI complementarity. Optimizing for human learning was harder.
what_is_learned: interaction policy (which form of assistance to give, conditioned on user and task state)
user_evidence: logged decisions and outcomes under different assistance types, user traits (e.g., need for cognition), task features
usil_relation: Closest existing example of a user-conditioned assistance policy learned with RL from interaction logs. Open question: can the policy be adapted online for a single user from that user's sparse evidence, rather than conditioned on population-level traits?

cite_role: Per-user assistance/autonomy mode from sparse feedback, transfers to new tasks
title: Robot Behavior Personalization from Sparse User Feedback
authors: Maithili Patel, Sonia Chernova
venue: IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (DOI 10.1109/LRA.2025.3550833); arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.19219
summary: TAACo is a task-adaptation module that sits on top of any robot policy. It predicts each user's preferred style of assistance per household task, including whether the robot should do the task at all or leave it to the user, by reasoning over abstract concepts built from sparse feedback. With 40 feedback samples per user it beat GPT-4 by 16% and a rule-based system by 54% in prediction accuracy, and it generalizes to unseen tasks.
user_evidence: Sparse user feedback on preferred assistance mode for household tasks
interaction_decisions: act / defer (do task autonomously, assist, or leave it to the user); explain (concept-based explanations)
usil_relation: This directly learns user-specific 'which steps to run autonomously' with cross-task transfer from sparse evidence. Remaining questions: does it adapt online to preference drift, and does the concept representation carry over to LLM agents working in software?

cite_role: Per-user permission (confirm vs act) prediction from 1–4 examples
title: Towards Automating Data Access Permissions in AI Agents
authors: Yuhao Wu, Ke Yang, Franziska Roesner, Tadayoshi Kohno, Ning Zhang, Umar Iqbal
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P) 2026
summary: Runs a user study of how people make data-access permission decisions for AI agents, then builds a personalized predictor of future decisions. The predictor combines in-context learning over the user's own permission history and attitudes with collaborative filtering over similar users. It reaches 85.1% accuracy overall and 94.4% on high-confidence predictions; adding just 1–4 history samples improves accuracy by 10.8 points over the no-history baseline.
user_evidence: Past allow/deny permission decisions, demographics, self-reported privacy and AI attitudes, and other users' decisions (collaborative filtering)
interaction_decisions: confirm / act (auto-grant vs. ask the user for permission)
usil_relation: This is close to learning pi_u for confirm-vs-act from sparse approvals and rejections. Open question: does a predictor of offline decisions remain calibrated when deployed live, as preferences drift and the agent's own auto-decisions change what evidence the user gives?

cite_role: Closest predecessor: interaction-preference benchmark and adaptation (PrefIx)
title: PrefIx: Understand and Adapt to User Preference in Human-Agent Interaction
authors: Jialin Li, Zhenhao Chen, Hanjun Luo, Hanan Salam
summary: Benchmark and methods for understanding and adapting to user preferences over human-agent interaction.
usil_relation: One of the closest predecessors (interaction preferences); check whether adaptation is longitudinal.

cite_role: Representative active preference-elicitation method; contrast what to ask with learning when to ask
title: Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models
authors: Belinda Z. Li, Alex Tamkin, Noah Goodman, Jacob Andreas
summary: GATE: LMs elicit task preferences by asking open-ended questions; outperforms user-written prompts.
usil_relation: Active elicitation per user; question budget and per-user cost of asking are open.

cite_role: Representative clarification-policy method; include if needed to distinguish when versus what to ask
title: Modeling Future Conversation Turns to Teach LLMs to Ask Clarifying Questions
authors: Michael J. Q. Zhang, W. Bradley Knox, Eunsol Choi
summary: Shows that preference labels judged only on prior context bias models toward presuming one interpretation; proposes double-turn preference annotation that scores responses by simulated outcomes in later turns, teaching models to ask clarifying questions only when it helps. Improves answer F1 on ambiguous QA and accuracy of the ask-vs-answer decision.
user_evidence: Annotated/simulated user answers to clarifying questions and resulting final-answer quality across multiple annotated interpretations
usil_relation: Directly tackles when-to-ask via future-turn credit assignment; remaining question is how to make the ask/answer threshold user-specific (some users prefer guesses, others prefer questions) from sparse feedback.

cite_role: Closest predecessor: multi-session collaboration preferences with memory
title: MultiSessionCollab: Learning User Preferences with Memory to Improve Long-Term Collaboration
authors: Shuhaib Mehri, Priyanka Kargupta, Tal August, Dilek Hakkani-Tür
summary: Agents learn user collaboration preferences across sessions with memory to improve long-term collaboration.
usil_relation: One of the closest predecessors; remaining question is explicit ask/act/defer decisions and transfer across tasks.

cite_role: Closest predecessor: clarification + per-user memory + feedback (PAHF)
title: Learning Personalized Agents from Human Feedback
authors: Kaiqu Liang, Julia Kruk, Shengyi Qian, Xianjun Yang, Shengjie Bi, Yuanshun Yao, Shaoliang Nie, Mingyang Zhang, Lijuan Liu, Jaime Fernández Fisac, Shuyan Zhou, Saghar Hosseini
summary: PAHF learns online per-user preferences via pre-action clarification, explicit per-user memory, and post-action feedback; introduces a four-phase evaluation protocol on manipulation and shopping.
user_evidence: answers to clarifying questions; post-action feedback
usil_relation: Very close to USIL (clarification + memory + feedback); open question is learning a per-user policy for when to ask, not only what to remember.

cite_role: Closest predecessor: policies conditioned on given interaction preferences (UserVille)
title: Training Proactive and Personalized LLM Agents
authors: Weiwei Sun, Xuhui Zhou, Weihua Du, et al. (incl. Graham Neubig, Maarten Sap, Yiming Yang)
summary: Defines Productivity, Proactivity and Personalization (PPP) as joint goals for agents, introduces UserVille (configurable LLM user simulators with diverse interaction preferences and user-centric feedback), and trains agents with multi-objective RL whose rewards cover task success, the cost of asking questions, and adherence to user preferences; agents improve on SWE-Bench and BrowseComp-Plus and generalize to unseen preferences.
user_evidence: simulated user answers to questions, user-centric feedback on preference adherence and effort, task outcome
interaction_decisions: ask, clarify, act (when to ask and how targeted the questions are; how to communicate)
usil_relation: Closest existing instance of training an interaction policy conditioned on user interaction preferences, but it conditions on a preference specified per episode by a simulator rather than learning it from an individual user's evidence across sessions.

cite_role: Closest predecessor: per-developer oversight policy learned across sessions
title: Hedwig: Dynamic Autonomy for Coding Agents Under Local Oversight
authors: Tanjal Shukla, K. J. Kevin Feng, Leijie Wang, Mohammad Rostami, Amy X. Zhang
venue: ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems (CAIS 2026), demo; arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.11495
summary: A formative survey of 21 engineers found that static permission settings and instruction files fail to track how oversight preferences shift across tasks and over time. Hedwig is a CLI coding agent that learns an evolving set of behavioral guidelines from developer decisions and feedback across sessions. It relaxes oversight where it has earned trust and tightens it in unfamiliar situations.
what_is_learned: interaction policy (evolving natural-language guidelines governing autonomy/oversight)
user_evidence: Developer approval/oversight decisions and feedback during coding sessions
interaction_decisions: act / confirm / defer (dynamic autonomy level, when to require approval)
usil_relation: This is nearly a direct USIL instance: a persistent, user-conditioned autonomy policy learned from approvals across sessions. Open questions: how well do the learned guidelines generalize to new task types, and how should they handle trust miscalibration after a costly error?

cite_role: Closest predecessor: user corrections compiled into persistent rules; title overlap
title: Getting Better at Working With You: Compiling User Corrections into Runtime Enforcement for Coding Agents
authors: Yujun Zhou, Kehan Guo, Haomin Zhuang, et al. (incl. Nitesh V. Chawla, Xiangliang Zhang)
summary: Shows that memory-based agents (e.g., Mem0) still violate 57.5% of a user's previously stated corrections; proposes TRACE, which extracts corrections from chat, turns them into atomic rules, and compiles them into runtime checks that must pass before a coding agent marks a task complete, cutting held-out violations sharply in and out of distribution.
what_is_learned: other: compiled per-user procedural rules / runtime checks
user_evidence: natural-language corrections in chat (anonymized real-user cases)
interaction_decisions: act, confirm (gating task completion on user-specific checks)
usil_relation: Very close to USIL's 'tell once' goal for procedural preferences across tasks; open question is whether corrections about the interaction itself (ask less, confirm before X) can be compiled the same way, and how rules are retired when preferences drift.

cite_role: Evaluation: per-user consent, intervention and restraint
title: KnowU-Bench: Towards Interactive, Proactive, and Personalized Mobile Agent Evaluation
authors: Tongbo Chen, Zhengxi Lu, Zhan Xu, et al.
summary: An online Android-emulator benchmark (42 general, 86 personalized, 64 proactive tasks) where the user profile is hidden and the agent must infer preferences from behavioral logs and multi-turn clarification with an LLM-simulated user; it scores GUI execution, consent negotiation and restraint after rejection, and finds that preference acquisition and intervention calibration, not GUI navigation, are the main bottlenecks.
what_is_learned: other: benchmark (evaluates inferred user model and intervention behavior)
user_evidence: behavioral logs, answers to clarification questions, consent and rejection responses
interaction_decisions: ask, clarify, intervene, confirm (consent), defer (restraint after rejection)
usil_relation: Directly evaluates per-user ask/intervene/consent decisions from inferred preferences, which makes it a candidate P4 testbed; it remains open whether agents improve these decisions over repeated sessions with the same user.

cite_role: Evaluation: long-term personalized and proactive agents
title: VitaBench 2.0: Evaluating Personalized and Proactive Agents in Long-Term User Interactions
authors: Yuxin Chen, Yi Zhang, Zhengzhou Cai, et al.
summary: A benchmark of time-ordered task sequences per user, with preferences scattered across interactions. Agents must keep extracting, applying and updating them, and must proactively spot missing information and get it from the user or the environment before deciding. Includes a pluggable memory interface for comparing architectures; even the strongest models struggle.
what_is_learned: other: evaluation benchmark (memory and user preferences)
user_evidence: Longitudinal per-user interaction histories with scattered, evolving preferences
usil_relation: Combines longitudinal per-user memory with ask-vs-infer evaluation, close to the USIL evaluation setting; open question: does it score whether the agent's asking behaviour adapts to the individual user (asking less once preferences are known), rather than gathering information uniformly?

cite_role: Alternative view: direct manipulation / explicit control suffices
title: Direct manipulation vs. interface agents
authors: Ben Shneiderman, Pattie Maes
summary: Classic debate: user-controlled direct manipulation versus autonomous interface agents that act on the user's behalf.

cite_role: Evaluation template for preference drift (content, not interaction)
title: Know Me, Respond to Me: Benchmarking LLMs for Dynamic User Profiling and Personalized Responses at Scale
authors: Bowen Jiang, Zhuoqun Hao, Young-Min Cho, et al. (incl. Lyle Ungar, Camillo J. Taylor, Dan Roth)
summary: Introduces PersonaMem: 180+ simulated users with up to 60 multi-turn sessions each across 15 tasks, testing whether LLMs track evolving traits and preferences and respond to the user's current state; frontier models reach only about 50% accuracy.
user_evidence: long multi-session conversation histories with preference changes over time
usil_relation: Provides an evaluation design for preference drift across sessions (P1), but only for response content; an analogous benchmark for drifting interaction preferences, such as a growing tolerance for autonomy, does not exist.

cite_role: Collaboration-process evaluation without per-user adaptation
title: Collaborative Gym: A Framework for Enabling and Evaluating Human-Agent Collaboration
authors: Yijia Shao, Vinay Samuel, Yucheng Jiang, John Yang, Diyi Yang
summary: Framework and environments for asynchronous human-agent collaboration with evaluation of outcomes and process.
usil_relation: Evaluates collaboration process, but not per-user adaptation.

cite_role: Representation locus: learned textual user summaries
title: Learning to Summarize User Information for Personalized Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
authors: Hyunji Nam, Yanming Wan, Mickel Liu, Jianxun Lian, Peter Ahnn, Natasha Jaques
summary: Learns textual user summaries that condition personalized reward models and policies.
usil_relation: Interpretable representation locus for USIL; could summaries capture procedural preferences?

cite_role: Alternative view: portable stated preferences instead of learning
title: Robust AI Personalization Will Require a Human Context Protocol
authors: Anand Shah, Tobin South, Talfan Evans, Hannah Rose Kirk, Andrew Trask, E. Glen Weyl, Michiel A. Bakker
summary: Position: personalization should rest on a user-owned, portable, natural-language preference layer shared across AI services.
usil_relation: Portable user context is a representation locus for USIL; open question is whether stated preferences suffice for interaction decisions.

cite_role: Alternative view: privacy and trust costs of personalization
title: Autonomy Reshapes How Personalization Affects Privacy Concerns and Trust in LLM Agents
authors: Zhiping Zhang, Yi Evie Zhang, Freda Shi, Tianshi Li
summary: A 3x3 between-subjects experiment (N=450) crossing agent autonomy level with personalization. A risk-contingent autonomy design, in which the agent returns control to the user when it detects possible privacy leakage, raises perceived control and dampens the rise in privacy concern and fall in trust that personalization otherwise causes. Introduces 'autonomy alignment' between user and agent decision authority.
what_is_learned: other: none learned (experimental comparison of autonomy designs)
user_evidence: self-reported privacy concern, trust, perceived control, willingness to use
usil_relation: Shows that returning control at risky moments raises perceived control, and points to a tension: the personal data USIL learns from can itself erode trust. Open question: can the triggers for returning control be learned per user while keeping user-model privacy costs acceptable?

cite_role: Sibling position paper (pluralistic alignment)
title: Position: A Roadmap to Pluralistic Alignment
authors: Taylor Sorensen et al.
summary: Position paper defining Overton, steerable, and distributional pluralism for aligning to diverse values.
usil_relation: Close in genre (position paper) and in arguing against averaging; focuses on values/outputs rather than how an agent works with a user.

cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
title: Learning to Clarify: Multi-turn Conversations with Action-Based Contrastive Self-Training
authors: Maximillian Chen, Ruoxi Sun, Tomas Pfister, Sercan Ö. Arık
summary: Proposes ACT, a quasi-online DPO variant that contrasts dialogue actions (clarify vs. answer) using on-policy multi-turn rollouts with a user simulator, learning data-efficient clarification policies; introduces AmbigSQL and evaluates on tabular QA and reading comprehension.
user_evidence: Small sets of conversations with implicit action labels plus simulated user replies during self-training
usil_relation: Shows that action-level preference learning can shape ask-vs-act from little data, a natural mechanism for few-shot user adaptation; untested whether per-user action preferences (from approvals/rejections) can be learned the same way.

cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
title: Bayesian Preference Elicitation with Language Models
authors: Kunal Handa, Yarin Gal, Ellie Pavlick, et al.
summary: Proposes OPEN, combining Bayesian optimal experimental design (to choose the most informative query over LM-extracted features) with an LM that verbalizes queries in natural language; user studies show better preference elicitation than LM-only or BOED-only baselines.
user_evidence: User answers to natural-language preference questions
usil_relation: Principled information-gain question selection with an explicit per-user posterior; open question is extending the posterior to interaction preferences (not just item preferences) and deciding when the information is worth the user's effort.

cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
title: When Users Change Their Mind: Evaluating Interruptible Agents in Long-Horizon Web Navigation
authors: Henry Peng Zou, Chunyu Miao, Wei-Chieh Huang, et al.
summary: Introduces InterruptBench (from WebArena-Lite) with three interruption types (addition, revision, retraction) mid-execution, evaluating how well six LLM agents adapt to updated goals and recover efficiently; finds interruption handling remains hard for strong models.
what_is_learned: other: benchmark of agent adaptation to user interruptions
user_evidence: Mid-task user interruptions (goal additions, revisions, retractions)
usil_relation: Treats interruptions as a feedback type agents must handle within a task; open question is whether interruption patterns can be learned as user evidence to anticipate a user's changes or to confirm earlier.

cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
title: STaR-GATE: Teaching Language Models to Ask Clarifying Questions
authors: Chinmaya Andukuri, Jan-Philipp Fränken, Tobias Gerstenberg, Noah D. Goodman
summary: Self-improvement loop that trains LMs to ask useful clarifying questions with simulated users.
usil_relation: Learns to ask well, but for a population of simulated users.

cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
title: Introspective Planning: Aligning Robots' Uncertainty with Inherent Task Ambiguity
authors: Kaiqu Liang, Zixu Zhang, Jaime Fernández Fisac
summary: Robots introspect over uncertainty to decide when to ask for clarification, with conformal guarantees.
usil_relation: Calibrated asking under ambiguity; thresholds are not user-specific.

cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
title: Tell Me More! Towards Implicit User Intention Understanding of Language Model Driven Agents
authors: Cheng Qian, Bingxiang He, Zhong Zhuang, et al.
summary: Introduces the Intention-in-Interaction (IN3) benchmark for detecting vague agent tasks and eliciting implicit user intentions through explicit questions, and trains Mistral-Interact as an upstream module that judges vagueness, queries missing details, and summarizes intent into goals before XAgent executes.
user_evidence: User answers to clarifying questions about missing task details (simulated and human)
interaction_decisions: clarify/ask vs. act; summarize intent before execution
